newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish govt disappointed over parade handling.
newsitem.headline: Irish govt disappointed over parade handling.

text.p: The Irish government said on Sunday it was deeply disappointed by Britain's decision to allow an Orange Order parade through a Catholic part of Portadown and had told the London authorities of its concern.

"The government have learned with deep disappointment of the decision in relation to the routing of the Orange parade in Portadown and have left the British government in no doubt about our serious concern for its implications," a statement said.

The statement said the confrontation underlined the need to draw up new rules governing disputed parades and should not deflect a three-year-old Anglo-Irish attempt to forge a negotiated settlement to the 28-year conflict.
Government sources said British Prime Minister Tony Blair told Ireland's new premier, Bertie Ahern of the decision to allow the parade to go ahead over Catholic objections.
Ahern, who took power last month promising to safeguard Irish nationalist rights in the British province, said last week that he would prefer that the parade be banned.
His remarks provoked outrage in the Orange Order, which accused him of trying to interfere in the affairs of the British province.

The statement said the Dublin government had backed efforts by Britain's Northern Ireland Secretary, Mo Mowlam, to find a compromise between the Orange Order and Catholics on the Garvaghy Road area of Portadown who wanted the parade stopped.
"We regret that our hopes for an agreed or acceptable solution on this occasion have been disappointed," the statement said.
Mowlam said police gave the parade the go-ahead to try to prevent violence on the scale provoked by last year's same parade, which provoked the worst civil strife in decades.

The statement called for restraint both from pro-British Loyalists and pro-Irish nationalists to avoid a repeat of last year's "debacle" when both sides rioted after the parade was initially banned then allowed to go ahead.

"The government understands the strong feelings which the decision to allow an Orange parade on the Garvaghy Road would arouse among the residents and in the wider nationalist community but in the difficult period ahead all concerned on both sides must act with dignity and restraint," it said.
"Above all, we must not allow this decision to deflect us from the search for peace," said the statement.
The two governments are co-sponsors of slow-moving Belfast peace talks aimed at reconciling the province's rival Loyalist and Nationalist traditions.
